source.text: וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Job and said:

en.L: And Job answered and said:
en.B: Then Job answered:
en.R: Then Job said:

decisions.choice: answered and said: the usual opening of a speech
decisions.reason: "He answered and said" introduces each speech in the dialogue (3:2; 4:1). Job answers Zophar's speech in chapter 20. This reply closes the second round of speeches.
Balanced and Readable use one English verb for the Hebrew pair, the book's pattern for speech introductions. The introduction stays prose.

source.text: שִׁמְע֣וּ שָׁ֭מוֹעַ מִלָּתִ֑י וּתְהִי־זֹ֝֗את תַּנְח֥וּמֹֽתֵיכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Listen, listening to my word, and let this be your consolations.

en.L: Listen, listen to my words, \q and let this be your consolation.
en.B: Listen carefully to what I say, \q and let that be the comfort you give me.
en.R: Just listen closely to what I am saying. \q That is the only comfort I want from you.

decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for force, as in 13:17, where Job used the same words.

decisions.choice: your consolations: the comfort you came to bring
decisions.reason: Tanchumot is comfort. The friends came to comfort Job (2:11), and Eliphaz asked if God's comforts were too small for him (15:11). Job says the only comfort he wants is that they listen; he had called them miserable comforters (16:2).
Literal keeps the doubled verb (m1); Balanced and Readable give its force with "carefully" and "closely".
Readable says plainly what Job asks (m2).

source.text: שָׂ֭אוּנִי וְאָנֹכִ֣י אֲדַבֵּ֑ר וְאַחַ֖ר דַּבְּרִ֣י תַלְעִֽיג׃

records.literal_gloss: Bear with me, and I, I will speak, and after my speaking you may mock.

en.L: Bear with me, and I will speak, \q and after I have spoken, you may mock.
en.B: Bear with me while I speak; \q then, when I have finished, go on mocking.
en.R: Be patient with me while I speak. \q After I have finished, you can go on making fun of me.

decisions.choice: you may mock: "you" here is singular
decisions.reason: The first line speaks to all the friends, but "you may mock" is singular. Job may be turning to Zophar, who has just spoken, or to each of them in turn.
Zophar had accused Job of mocking (11:3) and felt insulted by Job (20:3). Job turns the word back: let him mock once Job has had his say.
The pronoun "I" is written out: Job claims his own turn to speak.
Balanced and Readable say "go on", since the mocking has already begun.

source.text: הֶ֭אָנֹכִי לְאָדָ֣ם שִׂיחִ֑י וְאִם־מַ֝דּ֗וּעַ לֹא־תִקְצַ֥ר רוּחִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: As for me, [is] to a human my complaint? And if [so], why should my spirit not be short?

en.L: As for me, [is] my complaint to a human? \q And if [so], why should my spirit not be short?
en.B: As for me, is my complaint against a human being? \q Why then should I not be impatient?
en.R: Is it a human being I am complaining about? No! \q So why should I not be impatient?

decisions.choice: is my complaint to a human?: no, it is to God
decisions.reason: The question expects "no". Job's quarrel is with God, not with people (13:3; 16:20-21); that is why he cannot be calm.

decisions.choice: my spirit be short: be impatient
decisions.reason: A short spirit is impatience, the opposite of a long, patient spirit (Numbers 21:4; Micah 2:7; Proverbs 14:29).
Siach is a complaint or troubled musing, the word Job used for his laments (7:13; 10:1).
Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m2).
Readable gives the answer the question expects (m1).

source.text: פְּנוּ־אֵלַ֥י וְהָשַׁ֑מּוּ וְשִׂ֖ימוּ יָ֣ד עַל־פֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Turn to me and be appalled, and put a hand over a mouth.

en.L: Turn to me and be appalled, \q and put [your] hand over [your] mouth.
en.B: Look at me and be appalled; \q put your hand over your mouth.
en.R: Look at me and be shocked. \q Cover your mouth with your hand and say nothing.

decisions.choice: put your hand over your mouth: be silent
decisions.reason: A hand laid on the mouth is a sign of silence in shock or awe (29:9; 40:4; Judges 18:19; Micah 7:16).

decisions.choice: be appalled: be struck with horror
decisions.reason: The verb (shamem) means to be stunned or horrified. Job said the upright are appalled at his state (17:8).

decisions.choice: turn to me: look at me
decisions.reason: To turn to someone is to face and look at them (6:28).
Readable says what the gesture means (m1).

source.text: וְאִם־זָכַ֥רְתִּי וְנִבְהָ֑לְתִּי וְאָחַ֥ז בְּ֝שָׂרִ֗י פַּלָּצֽוּת׃

records.literal_gloss: And if I remember, I am dismayed, and shuddering takes hold of my flesh.

en.L: And when I remember, I am dismayed, \q and shuddering takes hold of my flesh.
en.B: When I think about it, I am terrified, \q and my whole body shudders.
en.R: When I think about it, I am filled with fear, \q and my body shakes.

decisions.choice: when I remember: when I think of what I am about to say
decisions.reason: What Job remembers is what follows: that the wicked live and prosper (21:7-13). It overturns everything the friends have said.
The verb (bahal) is used of sudden terror (4:5; 23:15).
Basar here is the body, which shakes with fear.

decisions.choice: my whole body shudders / my body shakes
alternatives: shuddering takes hold of my flesh
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make "body" the subject, which reads naturally in English.

source.text: מַדּ֣וּעַ רְשָׁעִ֣ים יִחְי֑וּ עָ֝תְק֗וּ גַּם־גָּ֥בְרוּ חָֽיִל׃

records.literal_gloss: Why do [the] wicked live, grow old, also grow mighty [in] strength?

en.L: Why do [the] wicked live, \q grow old, and even grow mighty in power?
en.B: Why do the wicked go on living, \q growing old and growing ever more powerful?
en.R: Why do wicked people go on living? \q Why do they live to old age and become more and more powerful?

decisions.choice: why do the wicked live?: the question the friends will not face
decisions.reason: All three friends have said that the wicked soon perish (8:13-19; 15:20-35; 18:5-21; 20:5-29). Job answers that what anyone can see is the opposite (compare Jeremiah 12:1; Psalm 73:3-12).

decisions.choice: grow old: live on, advance in years
decisions.reason: The verb ('ataq) means to move on or advance; here it is to grow old. Zophar had said the wicked die in their youthful vigor (20:11).
Chayil is strength, and also wealth (20:15, 18). Here, with "grow mighty", it is strength in every sense.
Readable repeats the question for each clause to keep the sentences short.

source.text: זַרְעָ֤ם נָכ֣וֹן לִפְנֵיהֶ֣ם עִמָּ֑ם וְ֝צֶאֱצָאֵיהֶ֗ם לְעֵינֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Their offspring [is] established before them with them, and their descendants before their eyes.

en.L: Their offspring [are] established before them, with them, \q and their descendants before their eyes.
en.B: Their children are settled securely around them; \q their descendants grow up before their eyes.
en.R: They see their children grow up and settle down near them. \q They live to see their children's children too.

decisions.choice: offspring and descendants: what the friends said the wicked would lose
decisions.reason: Bildad said the wicked have no offspring or descendants (18:19, the same two words), and Zophar that their children must beg from the poor (20:10). Eliphaz had promised the righteous many descendants (5:25).
Nakhon means firm, secure, lasting.
Balanced supplies a verb for the second line, which shares the verb of the first.
Readable says "children's children" for the descendants they live to see.

source.text: בָּתֵּיהֶ֣ם שָׁל֣וֹם מִפָּ֑חַד וְלֹ֤א שֵׁ֖בֶט אֱל֣וֹהַּ עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Their houses [are] peace from fear, and the rod of God [is] not on them.

en.L: Their houses [are] safe from fear, \q and the rod of God [is] not upon them.
en.B: Their homes are safe and free from fear; \q the rod of God does not strike them.
en.R: Their homes are safe, and they have nothing to fear. \q God does not punish them.

decisions.reason: Shalom here is safety and well-being. Eliphaz promised the righteous that their tent would be at peace (5:24).

decisions.choice: the rod of God: his punishment
decisions.reason: The rod is a picture of God's discipline and punishment (9:34; Psalm 89:33). Job had asked God to take his rod away from him (9:34); the wicked do not even feel it.
"From" means away from: nothing threatens them.

alternatives: the rod of God is not upon them
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the picture (m2).

source.text: שׁוֹר֣וֹ עִ֭בַּר וְלֹ֣א יַגְעִ֑ל תְּפַלֵּ֥ט פָּ֝רָת֗וֹ וְלֹ֣א תְשַׁכֵּֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: His bull breeds and does not fail; his cow calves and does not miscarry.

en.L: His bull breeds and does not fail; \q his cow calves and does not miscarry.
en.B: Their bulls breed without fail; \q their cows calve and never miscarry.
en.R: Their bulls always breed, \q and their cows have calves and never lose them.

decisions.reason: The pronoun is singular, meaning each one of them.
The verb (ga'al in this form) is rare; it means to fail or to reject. The bull never fails to make a cow pregnant.

decisions.choice: does not miscarry: the blessing of the obedient
decisions.reason: God promised his people that none among them or their animals would miscarry or be barren (Exodus 23:26; Deuteronomy 7:14). Job sees that blessing given to the wicked.
Balanced and Readable say "their" for the singular that means each of them (m1).

source.text: יְשַׁלְּח֣וּ כַ֭צֹּאן עֲוִילֵיהֶ֑ם וְ֝יַלְדֵיהֶ֗ם יְרַקֵּדֽוּן׃

records.literal_gloss: They send out like a flock their little ones, and their children dance.

en.L: They send out their little ones like a flock, \q and their children dance.
en.B: They let their little ones run out like a flock of lambs, \q and their children skip about.
en.R: Their little children run out to play like lambs, \q and they dance around.

decisions.reason: 'Avil is a young child (19:18).
The verb (raqad) is used of lambs and rams skipping (Psalm 114:4, 6) and of children at play.

decisions.choice: their children: Job's own were killed
decisions.reason: Job's own sons and daughters died together (1:18-19); the children of the wicked play in safety.

decisions.choice: a flock of lambs / like lambs
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "lambs" so the picture of young animals running free is clear.

source.text: יִ֭שְׂאוּ כְּתֹ֣ף וְכִנּ֑וֹר וְ֝יִשְׂמְח֗וּ לְק֣וֹל עוּגָֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: They lift [voices] with tambourine and lyre, and rejoice at the sound of a flute.

en.L: They lift [their voices] to tambourine and lyre, \q and rejoice at [the] sound of [the] flute.
en.B: They sing to the tambourine and the lyre \q and make merry at the sound of the flute.
en.R: They sing along with the tambourine and the harp, \q and they have fun listening to the flute.

decisions.reason: "Lift" without an object means to lift the voice in song (Isaiah 24:14; 42:11).

decisions.choice: tambourine, lyre and flute: instruments of celebration
decisions.reason: The tof is a hand drum or tambourine (Exodus 15:20); the kinnor is a lyre and the 'ugav a pipe or flute (Genesis 4:21). Job will say his own lyre and flute have turned to mourning (30:31).
Readable says "harp", the stringed instrument most readers know; Literal and Balanced say "lyre".

source.text: יְכַלּ֣וּ בַטּ֣וֹב יְמֵיהֶ֑ם וּ֝בְרֶ֗גַע שְׁא֣וֹל יֵחָֽתּוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: They complete in good their days, and in a moment [to] Sheol they go down.

en.L: They spend their days in prosperity, \q and in a moment they go down [to] Sheol.
en.B: They live out their days in prosperity \q and go down to Sheol in an instant.
en.R: They enjoy good lives all their days. \q Then they die quickly, without suffering, and go down to the grave.

decisions.reason: The consonants as written give "they wear out" their days; the reading the scribes marked gives "they complete" them. Elihu uses the read form in the same phrase, "they complete their days in prosperity" (36:11). Either way they live out their days in comfort.

decisions.choice: in a moment: a quick death, without long suffering
decisions.reason: Rega' is a moment (20:5); a word with the same letters can mean rest, which would give "in peace". Either way their death is easy. Zophar had said the joy of the wicked lasts only a moment (20:5); Job says their dying takes only a moment.

decisions.choice: Sheol: the place of the dead
decisions.reason: Sheol is the place where all the dead go (7:9; 14:13; 17:13).
Readable says "the grave" for Sheol, the book's choice.
Readable says what a death "in a moment" means (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ לָ֭אֵל ס֣וּר מִמֶּ֑נּוּ וְדַ֥עַת דְּ֝רָכֶ֗יךָ לֹ֣א חָפָֽצְנוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And they say to God: Depart from us, and the knowledge of your ways we do not desire.

en.L: And they say to God, "Turn away from us; \q we do not desire [the] knowledge of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} ways.
en.B: Yet they say to God, "Leave us alone! \q We have no wish to know {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} ways.
en.R: Yet they tell God, "Go away and leave us alone! \q We do not want to know how {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} want us to live.

decisions.choice: and they say: yet, all the while, they say
decisions.reason: The "and" sets their words against all the blessings just listed: this is how they answer God. Their words run on through verse 15.

decisions.choice: the knowledge of your ways: knowing how God wants people to live
decisions.reason: God's ways are the way of life he teaches (Psalm 25:4; Exodus 33:13).

decisions.choice: depart from us: words Eliphaz will quote back
decisions.reason: Eliphaz repeats these words in his reply (22:17).
Balanced and Readable show the contrast (m1).

decisions.choice: how you want us to live
decisions.reason: Readable says what God's ways are (m2).

source.text: מַה־שַׁדַּ֥י כִּֽי־נַֽעַבְדֶ֑נּוּ וּמַה־נּ֝וֹעִ֗יל כִּ֣י נִפְגַּע־בּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: What [is] the Almighty that we should serve him, and what will we gain that we entreat him?

en.L: What [is] the Almighty, that we should serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}? \q And what will we gain if we pray to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?"
en.B: Who is the Almighty, that we should serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}? \q What good will it do us to pray to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?"
en.R: Who is God All-Powerful, that we should serve {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}? \q What would we get out of praying to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}?"

decisions.choice: What is the Almighty?: a scornful question
decisions.reason: "What" rather than "who" belittles God: what is he to us? Pharaoh spoke of God with the same scorn (Exodus 5:2).

decisions.choice: what will we gain?: serving God for profit
decisions.reason: The Accuser asked whether Job feared God for nothing (1:9). The wicked serve God only if it pays, and decide it does not; Job, who has lost everything, still holds on to God.

decisions.choice: pray to him: plead with him
decisions.reason: The verb (paga') means to meet, and so to approach someone with a plea (Jeremiah 7:16; Ruth 1:16).
Balanced and Readable say "Who", the natural English question about a person; Literal keeps "What" (m1).
Readable says "God All-Powerful" for Shaddai, the book's choice (5:17).

source.text: הֵ֤ן לֹ֣א בְיָדָ֣ם טוּבָ֑ם עֲצַ֥ת רְ֝שָׁעִ֗ים רָ֣חֲקָה מֶֽנִּי׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, not in their hand [is] their prosperity; the counsel of [the] wicked is far from me.

en.L: Look, their prosperity [is] not in their own hand; \q the counsel of [the] wicked is far from me.
en.B: Yet their prosperity is not in their own hands. \q The advice of the wicked is far from me.
en.R: But they did not get their good fortune by their own power. \q I want nothing to do with the plans of wicked people.

decisions.choice: their prosperity is not in their own hand: it comes from God
alternatives: Is not their prosperity in their own hand?
decisions.reason: As a statement, Job says the wicked did not make their own good fortune: God gave it to them, which is what troubles him. It may also be a question, "Is not their prosperity in their own hand?", meaning they hold it securely. Either way the wicked prosper.

decisions.choice: the counsel of the wicked is far from me: I do not share their outlook
decisions.reason: Though he says the wicked prosper, Job refuses their way of thinking (Psalm 1:1). Eliphaz repeats the line in 22:18.
Tuv is the good fortune that Zophar said would not last (20:21).

decisions.choice: I want nothing to do with
decisions.reason: Readable says what keeping the plans far away means (m2).

source.text: כַּמָּ֤ה׀נֵר־רְשָׁ֘עִ֤ים יִדְעָ֗ךְ וְיָבֹ֣א עָלֵ֣ימוֹ אֵידָ֑ם חֲ֝בָלִ֗ים יְחַלֵּ֥ק בְּאַפּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: How often [is] the lamp of [the] wicked put out, and comes on them their calamity? Pains he apportions in his anger?

en.L: How often is the lamp of [the] wicked put out, \q and [how often] does their disaster come upon them? \q [How often does] {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} deal out pains in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger?
en.B: How often is the lamp of the wicked snuffed out? \q How often does disaster fall on them, \q or God deal out sorrows in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger?
en.R: How often does the lamp of the wicked really go out? \q How often does disaster strike them, \q or God punish them in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger?

decisions.choice: the lamp of the wicked put out: Bildad's words
decisions.reason: Bildad said the lamp of the wicked is put out and disaster stands ready for him (18:5-6, 12), using the same words. A lamp going out is a life or a family line coming to an end.
The question expects the answer "seldom"; it governs verse 18 as well.

decisions.choice: pains he deals out: a play on words
decisions.reason: Chavalim are pains, like the pangs of birth; the same letters also mean shares or portions, and the verb chillek is "to divide out". God, who is said to give the wicked their share (20:29), seldom deals them pain.
The subject of "deals out" is God, as "his anger" shows.
Balanced and Readable name God (m4).
Readable adds "really" to show the doubt the question expresses (m2).

source.text: יִהְי֗וּ כְּתֶ֥בֶן לִפְנֵי־ר֑וּחַ וּ֝כְמֹ֗ץ גְּנָבַ֥תּוּ סוּפָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: [Are] they like straw before a wind, and like chaff [that] a storm steals away?

en.L: [Are] they like straw before [the] wind, \q and like chaff that [the] storm carries off?
en.B: How often are they like straw before the wind, \q like chaff swept away by a storm?
en.R: How often are they blown away like straw in the wind, \q or like chaff carried off by a storm?

decisions.choice: straw and chaff: the fate the wicked are said to meet
decisions.reason: The wicked are like chaff the wind drives away (Psalm 1:4; 35:5). Job asks how often that really happens.
The question of verse 17 carries on into this verse.
The verb (ganav) is "to steal"; a storm carries off the chaff as a thief would (27:20).
Balanced and Readable repeat "How often" from verse 17 (m2).

source.text: אֱל֗וֹהַּ יִצְפֹּן־לְבָנָ֥יו אוֹנ֑וֹ יְשַׁלֵּ֖ם אֵלָ֣יו וְיֵדָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: God stores up for his children his iniquity; let him repay to him, so that he knows.

en.L: God stores up his iniquity for his children. \q Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} repay [the man] himself, so that he knows [it]!
en.B: You say, "God stores up their punishment for their children." \q Let God repay the wicked themselves, so that they feel it!
en.R: You say that God saves up the punishment of the wicked for their children. \q But God should punish the wicked themselves, so that they know what their sin deserves!

decisions.choice: God stores up ...: the friends' view, quoted by Job
decisions.reason: The first line is what the friends have been saying (5:4; 20:10): if the wicked escape, their children will pay. Job answers it in the second line. Hebrew often quotes without saying "you say".

decisions.choice: his iniquity: the punishment for his iniquity
decisions.reason: 'Awen is wrongdoing and the trouble it brings; here it is the penalty for the wrong.

decisions.choice: let him repay him, so that he knows: Job's demand
decisions.reason: The verb is a wish or demand: God should pay back the wrongdoer himself, so that he feels it. Punishing children for their parents' sin does not touch the guilty (Deuteronomy 24:16; Ezekiel 18:20).
Balanced and Readable add "You say" so the reader can follow the quotation (m1); Literal leaves it unmarked, as the Hebrew does.
Literal brackets the words English needs to show who is repaid.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person, as the plural "the wicked" of 21:7 shows. Balanced and Readable use "they"; Literal follows the Hebrew "he".

source.text: יִרְא֣וּ עֵינָ֣יו כִּיד֑וֹ וּמֵחֲמַ֖ת שַׁדַּ֣י יִשְׁתֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Let his eyes see his ruin, and of the wrath of the Almighty let him drink.

en.L: Let his [own] eyes see his ruin, \q and let him drink of the wrath of the Almighty.
en.B: Let them see their own ruin with their own eyes; \q let them drink the wrath of the Almighty.
en.R: Wicked people should see their own ruin with their own eyes. \q They should have to drink the anger of God All-Powerful.

decisions.reason: Kid occurs only here; it means disaster or ruin.

decisions.choice: drink the wrath: suffer God's anger in full
decisions.reason: God's anger is pictured as a cup the guilty must drink (Psalm 75:9; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15).

decisions.choice: let him see ... let him drink: Job's wish
decisions.reason: Job carries on the demand of verse 19: the guilty themselves should suffer.
Readable says "God All-Powerful" for Shaddai, the book's choice (5:17).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person, as the plural "the wicked" of 21:7 shows. Balanced and Readable use "they"; Literal follows the Hebrew "he".

source.text: כִּ֤י מַה־חֶפְצ֣וֹ בְּבֵית֣וֹ אַחֲרָ֑יו וּמִסְפַּ֖ר חֳדָשָׁ֣יו חֻצָּֽצוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For what [is] his pleasure in his house after him, and the number of his months is cut off?

en.L: For what [does] he care about his house after him, \q when the number of his months has been cut off?
en.B: For what do they care about their family after they are gone, \q when the number of their months has run out?
en.R: What do they care about what happens to their family after they die, \q when their time is over?

decisions.reason: Chefets is delight or interest (22:3). Once a man is dead, what happens to his family does not concern him (14:21).

decisions.choice: the number of his months: his lifetime
decisions.reason: Job said God had set the number of a person's months (14:5).

decisions.choice: for: why punishing the children is no answer
decisions.reason: This gives the reason for verses 19-20: the dead do not feel what happens to their children.
Balanced and Readable say "family", which is what "house" means here.
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person, as the plural "the wicked" of 21:7 shows. Balanced and Readable use "they"; Literal follows the Hebrew "he".

source.text: הַלְאֵ֥ל יְלַמֶּד־דָּ֑עַת וְ֝ה֗וּא רָמִ֥ים יִשְׁפּֽוֹט׃

records.literal_gloss: To God will one teach knowledge, and he judges those on high?

en.L: Will anyone teach knowledge to God, \q since {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} judges [those] on high?
en.B: Can anyone teach God knowledge, \q when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} judges even those on high?
en.R: Can anyone teach God anything? \q He judges even those in the highest places.

decisions.choice: those on high: the highest beings
decisions.reason: Ramim are the high or lofty: heavenly beings (4:18; 15:15; 25:2), or the powerful on earth. If God judges even them, no one can tell him how to rule.

decisions.choice: will anyone teach God?: no one can
decisions.reason: The question expects "no" (compare Isaiah 40:13-14). Job may be answering the friends, who presume to know how God must treat the wicked, or voicing their objection to him; the Hebrew does not mark which.
The pronoun is written out: it is God himself who judges.

source.text: זֶ֗ה יָ֭מוּת בְּעֶ֣צֶם תֻּמּ֑וֹ כֻּ֝לּ֗וֹ שַׁלְאֲנַ֥ן וְשָׁלֵֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: This [one] dies in the bone of his completeness, all of him at ease and quiet.

en.L: One dies in his full vigor, \q wholly at ease and secure.
en.B: One person dies in full vigor, \q completely secure and at ease.
en.R: Some people die while still strong and healthy, \q completely comfortable and free from worry.

decisions.choice: this one ... that one: two lives set side by side
decisions.reason: "This one" here and "that one" in verse 25 compare two people who meet the same end (21:26).

decisions.choice: in the bone of his completeness: in full health
decisions.reason: "The bone of" means the very substance: in the fullness of his strength. Tom, completeness, comes from the same root as "blameless" in 1:1, but here it means soundness of body.
Sha'anan and shalev are near synonyms for living untroubled (16:12 uses shalev of Job's own former ease).
The Hebrew speaks of any person; Balanced and Readable avoid "he", Literal keeps "his".

source.text: עֲ֭טִינָיו מָלְא֣וּ חָלָ֑ב וּמֹ֖חַ עַצְמוֹתָ֣יו יְשֻׁקֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: His pails are full of milk, and the marrow of his bones is watered.

en.L: His pails are full of milk, \q and the marrow of his bones is moist.
en.B: Their pails are full of milk, \q and their bones are rich with marrow.
en.R: They have plenty of milk, \q and their bodies are healthy and strong.

decisions.reason: 'Atin occurs only here. It may be a pail, so that he has milk in plenty, or a part of the body, so that his body is well fed; with the vowels of chelev for chalav, "milk" becomes "fat". The second line speaks of the body.
Marrow in the bones is a picture of health (Proverbs 3:8). Dry bones are the opposite (Proverbs 17:22).

decisions.choice: their bodies are healthy and strong
alternatives: the marrow of their bones is moist
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the picture (m2).
Balanced and Readable say "their" for the person of verse 23.

source.text: וְזֶ֗ה יָ֭מוּת בְּנֶ֣פֶשׁ מָרָ֑ה וְלֹֽא־אָ֝כַ֗ל בַּטּוֹבָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And this [one] dies with a bitter soul and has not eaten of good.

en.L: And another dies with a bitter soul \q and has never tasted [anything] good.
en.B: Another dies in bitterness of soul, \q never having tasted anything good.
en.R: Other people die bitter and unhappy, \q never having enjoyed anything good.

decisions.reason: The second "this one" is the other of the pair begun in verse 23.
Job used the same words of himself (7:11; 10:1) and of those who long for death (3:20).

decisions.choice: eaten of good: enjoyed good things
decisions.reason: To eat of good is to enjoy a good life (Ecclesiastes 6:2, 6).
Balanced and Readable choose verbs that fit "anything good" in English.

source.text: יַ֭חַד עַל־עָפָ֣ר יִשְׁכָּ֑בוּ וְ֝רִמָּ֗ה תְּכַסֶּ֥ה עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Together on dust they lie, and the maggot covers over them.

en.L: Together they lie down in the dust, \q and [the] worm covers them.
en.B: They lie down alike in the dust, \q and worms cover them both.
en.R: In the end both are buried in the dust, \q and worms cover them.

decisions.choice: lie in the dust: die and be buried
decisions.reason: To lie in the dust is to be in the grave (7:21; 20:11).
Rimmah is the maggot that feeds on the dead (17:14; 24:20; Isaiah 14:11).

decisions.choice: together: death makes no difference between them
decisions.reason: The happy and the bitter end alike; their deaths show nothing of who deserved what (Ecclesiastes 9:2-3).
Readable makes plain that the two people of verses 23-25 are meant.

source.text: הֵ֣ן יָ֭דַעְתִּי מַחְשְׁבֽוֹתֵיכֶ֑ם וּ֝מְזִמּ֗וֹת עָלַ֥י תַּחְמֹֽסוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Look, I know your thoughts and the schemes [with which] against me you do violence.

en.L: Look, I know your thoughts, \q and the schemes [with which] you would wrong me.
en.B: Look, I know what you are thinking, \q the schemes you plot to wrong me.
en.R: I know what you are thinking. \q I know how you are planning to hurt me.

decisions.reason: Chamas is violence or injustice; Job used it of the wrong done to him (16:17; 19:7).
Mezimmot are plans or plots (Psalm 37:7). Job sees where their portraits of the wicked are aimed: at him.
Job now speaks to all the friends again.

source.text: כִּ֤י תֹֽאמְר֗וּ אַיֵּ֥ה בֵית־נָדִ֑יב וְ֝אַיֵּ֗ה אֹ֤הֶל׀מִשְׁכְּנ֬וֹת רְשָׁעִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: For you say: Where [is] the house of the noble, and where [is] the tent of the dwellings of [the] wicked?

en.L: For you say, "Where [is] the house of the prince? \q And where [is] the tent, the dwelling place of [the] wicked?"
en.B: For you say, "Where now is the prince's house? \q Where are the tents where the wicked lived?"
en.R: You say, "What happened to that powerful man's house? \q Where are the homes where those wicked people lived?"

decisions.choice: the prince: the great man, here a rich oppressor
decisions.reason: Nadiv is a noble or prince (12:21; 34:18). Set beside "the wicked", it is the powerful man who did wrong.

decisions.choice: Where is his house?: aimed at Job
decisions.reason: The friends said the tent of the wicked would be gone (8:22; 15:34; 18:15, 21; 20:26-28). Job's own house fell on his children (1:19); he knows whom they mean.

decisions.choice: you say: Job quotes the friends
decisions.reason: The questions are the friends' words: the house of the wicked always disappears.
Readable says "that powerful man" to show the hint at Job (m2).

source.text: הֲלֹ֣א שְׁ֭אֶלְתֶּם ע֣וֹבְרֵי דָ֑רֶךְ וְ֝אֹתֹתָ֗ם לֹ֣א תְנַכֵּֽרוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Have you not asked those passing on the road, and their signs do you not recognize?

en.L: Have you not asked those who pass along the road? \q And do you not recognize their accounts?
en.B: Have you never asked people who travel the roads? \q Do you not accept what they report?
en.R: Have you never asked travelers what they have seen? \q Surely you know the stories they tell.

decisions.choice: those who pass along the road: travelers who have seen the world
decisions.reason: Travelers bring news from many places. Job sets their experience against the friends' appeal to the tradition of the elders (8:8; 15:18).
'Otot are signs, here the evidence travelers point to: what they have seen and report.
The verb (nakar) means to recognize or acknowledge.
Readable turns the second question into the statement it implies.

source.text: כִּ֤י לְי֣וֹם אֵ֭יד יֵחָ֣שֶׂךְ רָ֑ע לְי֖וֹם עֲבָר֣וֹת יוּבָֽלוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: That to a day of calamity the evil [one] is spared; to a day of furies they are led.

en.L: that on [the] day of calamity the evil [one] is spared, \q on [the] day of wrath they are led [to safety].
en.B: that the evil are spared on the day of disaster \q and led to safety on the day of wrath.
en.R: They will tell you that when disaster comes, evil people escape it; \q when the day of fury comes, they are led away to safety.

decisions.reason: "That" introduces what the travelers of verse 29 have seen.

decisions.choice: on the day of disaster the evil are spared
alternatives: the evil are kept for the day of disaster, led out to the day of wrath
decisions.reason: The preposition le- can mean "on" or "for". Read as "on", the evil are spared when disaster strikes, which is Job's point and what verses 31-33 go on to say. Read as "for", they are kept for a day of judgment, which would be the friends' view.
'Evrot is the plural of fury: the day when anger breaks out.
The Hebrew says only "they are led"; Literal brackets where to (m2).
Readable starts a new sentence and says whose report this is (m1).

source.text: מִֽי־יַגִּ֣יד עַל־פָּנָ֣יו דַּרְכּ֑וֹ וְהֽוּא־עָ֝שָׂ֗ה מִ֣י יְשַׁלֶּם־לֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Who will declare to his face his way? And [what] he has done, who will repay him?

en.L: Who declares his way to his face? \q And [for] what he has done, who repays him?
en.B: Who confronts them to their face about the way they live? \q Who pays them back for what they have done?
en.R: No one dares to tell them to their face how wrong they are. \q No one pays them back for what they have done.

decisions.reason: Both questions expect the answer "no one": the powerful wrongdoer is never called to account.

decisions.choice: declare his way to his face: accuse him openly
decisions.reason: To tell a person his way to his face is to confront him with how he lives.

decisions.choice: repay: pay back what is due
decisions.reason: The verb (shillem) is the one Job used in verse 19: let God repay the wrongdoer himself. Here no one does.
Readable turns the questions into the statements they mean (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person, as the plural "the wicked" of 21:7 shows. Balanced and Readable use "they"; Literal follows the Hebrew "he".

source.text: וְ֭הוּא לִקְבָר֣וֹת יוּבָ֑ל וְֽעַל־גָּדִ֥ישׁ יִשְׁקֽוֹד׃

records.literal_gloss: And he to [the] graves is carried, and over a tomb one keeps watch.

en.L: And he is carried to the grave, \q and over [his] tomb [someone] keeps watch.
en.B: They are carried in procession to the grave, \q and a watch is kept over their tomb.
en.R: When they die, they are carried to the grave in a grand funeral, \q and people keep guard over their tomb.

decisions.choice: carried to the grave, a watch kept: an honored burial
decisions.reason: He is borne in procession to the burial place, and someone watches over his tomb. The wicked man receives the honor of a great funeral and a guarded grave.
Gadish is a heap, used of a stack of grain (5:26); here it is a tomb or burial mound.
The same verb (yuval) was used in verse 30: the evil are led away to safety on the day of wrath, and at the end are carried to an honored grave.

decisions.choice: in procession / in a grand funeral
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what kind of carrying is meant (m1).
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person, as the plural "the wicked" of 21:7 shows. Balanced and Readable use "they"; Literal follows the Hebrew "he".

source.text: מָֽתְקוּ־ל֗וֹ רִגְבֵ֫י נָ֥חַל וְ֭אַחֲרָיו כָּל־אָדָ֣ם יִמְשׁ֑וֹךְ וּ֝לְפָנָ֗יו אֵ֣ין מִסְפָּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Sweet to him are the clods of the valley, and after him every human draws, and before him there is no number.

en.L: The clods of the valley are sweet to him; \q and after him every {{gender:person|man}} draws [along], \q and before him [are those] without number.
en.B: The soil of the valley lies gently on them; \q everyone walks behind in the procession, \q and countless people go ahead.
en.R: The soil of the valley rests softly on them. \q Everyone walks behind the body in the funeral procession, \q and crowds go ahead of it.

decisions.choice: the clods are sweet to him: he rests in peace
decisions.reason: The earth of the grave lies pleasantly on him. Even in death he is at ease.

decisions.choice: the valley: a wadi, a dry riverbed
decisions.reason: Nachal is a valley with a stream that runs only in the rainy season; tombs were often cut in the sides of such valleys.

decisions.choice: a funeral crowd behind him and before him
alternatives: all people will follow him in death, as countless went before him
decisions.reason: The lines most likely continue the funeral of verse 32: everyone joins the procession behind the body, and a crowd without number goes in front. They may also say that all people will follow him in death, as countless others died before him; either way he meets no worse an end than anyone else.
'Adam is a human being, man or woman; Literal uses the gender setting, and Balanced and Readable say "everyone".
The Hebrew singular means any wicked person, as the plural "the wicked" of 21:7 shows. Balanced and Readable use "they"; Literal follows the Hebrew "he".

source.text: וְ֭אֵיךְ תְּנַחֲמ֣וּנִי הָ֑בֶל וּ֝תְשֽׁוּבֹתֵיכֶ֗ם נִשְׁאַר־מָֽעַל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And how will you comfort me [with] vanity? And of your answers there remains unfaithfulness.

en.L: And how will you comfort me [with] emptiness? \q And of your answers, [only] treachery remains.
en.B: So how can you comfort me with empty words? \q Nothing is left of your answers but falsehood.
en.R: So how can your empty words comfort me? \q All your answers are lies.

decisions.reason: Hevel is a breath of air, something with no substance (7:16; 9:29; Ecclesiastes 1:2).

Ma'al is unfaithfulness, the word for breaking faith with God or with a person (Leviticus 5:15; Joshua 7:1). The friends' answers betray the friendship they came to show, and what they say is false to the facts.

decisions.choice: comfort me: the friends came to comfort
decisions.reason: Job ends where he began (21:2): the friends came to comfort him (2:11), but their comfort is empty.
Balanced and Readable say what the answers amount to in plain English; Literal keeps the sense of broken faith (m2).
